Part A — Creating Data Frames
```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

```{r}
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
students
```

```{r}
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```

```{r}
courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)
courses
```
Question #1

You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline.
Both approaches produce the same kind of object.
In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.

    Since a data frame is a grid of rows and columns, each row must have the same number of elements in each column. An error such as "arguments imply differing number of rows" would occur if columns had different lengths because R would not know how to fill in the gaps in the table.

Question #2

A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.”
Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

    Each element of a data frame, which is organized as a list, is a vector that represents a column. While a list can hold entirely different objects together, a single vector in R must contain elements of the exact same data type. This makes it possible for one column to be logical, one to be numeric, and one to be character text.

Question #3

students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects.
Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.

    Because the $ symbol extracts the raw vector from the data frame, running class(students$age) yields "numeric". Because single brackets [] slice the data frame and return a smaller data frame structure containing that column, running class(students",age"] yields "data.frame."

Question #4

In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows.
What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

    Only when both conditions are satisfied simultaneously does the & operator return TRUE after checking both condition vectors position by position. R would return rows where a student passed or was older than 19 if you used | (OR) instead, including students who only satisfied one of the two requirements.

Question #5

Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name).
Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

    R computes standard summary statistics (min, max, mean, median) for numerical columns such as age. R counts the number of TRUE and FALSE values for logical columns such as passed. R displays fundamental attributes like length and class for character columns like name. Since letters cannot be added or averaged numerically, it is illogical to calculate a "mean" for text names.

Question #6

str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information.
Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

    When examining a dataset's structure, column types, and data format, str() is more helpful. When you want a brief statistical summary or distribution of the actual values within the dataset, summary() is useful.

```{r}
students
```

```{r}
students
```

```{r}
students[order(students$age), ]
```

```{r}
students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
Question #7

After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)?
Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

    No, since the passed column is no longer present, running students$passed == TRUE would either fail or return logical(0). This demonstrates why monitoring changes is crucial: if a column is removed, any scripts or subsequent steps that depend on it will fail.

Question #8

order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions.
Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

    order(students$age) examines the age values and returns the row positions in ascending order (e.g., 3, 1, 5, 2, 4). R pulls the rows in that particular order across all columns at once when that vector is passed into the row slot students[...,].
    
Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

grades$drop <- grades$midterm - grades$final

grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 80, "Passed", "Failed")

grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```
Question #9

Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”
Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

    To measure grade drops, I will first make a new column called drop calculating midterm-final. Next, separate the students who got a "Failed" comment by filtering the dataset. Next, contrast the midterm results of the students who failed with their grade reductions. Finally, sort the table by midterm and drop to see if failing students began with low midterm scores or experienced a significant decline on the final.
    
Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what a data frame is, how it relates to vectors and lists from earlier labs, and why it is R’s primary structure for real-world tabular data.

    R's main tabular data structure is a data frame, which is made up of equal-length vectors arranged as rows and columns. Each column can hold a different kind of data because it combines the capabilities of lists, which store multiple data types together, and vectors, which hold single data types. Data frames offer the best structure for data analysis in R because real-world data typically comes in tables with mixed types (such as names, ages, and statuses).
